title: Bring in ‘cosmetic cowboys’ law to avoid more deaths, says family of butt lift victim
summary:
Relatives speak out as inquest jury find Alice Webb’s death after filler entered her organs was accidental

The family of a woman who died after a botched Brazilian butt lift have called for…

blocks.text: The family of a woman who died after a botched Brazilian butt lift have called for laws against “cosmetic cowboys” to be introduced before more people lose their lives.
Speaking as an inquest jury concluded Alice Webb’s death was accidental, her family said they were astonished people were still having BBLs despite what had happened to her.
Webb, 33, collapsed and died after undergoing a BBL by Jordan Parke, known as the “Lip King”, at a treatment room in Gloucestershire.
Jurors were told Parke injected Webb with seven times the amount of filler he had been taught to use, and a postmortem found traces of the gel-like substance in her heart, lung, kidneys and brain.

blocks.caption: Jordan Parke, pictured on the This Morning TV programme in 2015, died this year. Photograph: Ken McKay/ITV/Shutterstock

blocks.text: The procedure took place in a small treatment room in a semi-detached house which did not have equipment such as ultrasound probes to help a practitioner ensure they were injecting the correct layer of skin. There was no life-saving kit on hand.

Speaking outside the Gloucestershire coroner’s court, Webb’s family said they wanted an “Alice’s law” to be brought in as soon as possible. April Palmer, Webb’s sister, said: “We’d like to see tighter regulation, more protection.”
She said it was astounding that people were still having BBLs. “We need the government to take urgent action. We believe it could prevent avoidable harm and spare other families the same heartbreak.”

blocks.caption: Alice Webb’s sister, April Palmer, and her former partner, Ben Kingscote, outside the coroner’s court during the inquest.

blocks.text: Palmer said her sister had struggled with “low self-worth” and subjected herself to cosmetic procedures as she sought “elusive perfection”.
Last month, the UK government announced what it billed a “cosmetic cowboys crackdown” for England that includes only allowing doctors to carry out BBLs. It is currently consulting on its plans.

Ben Kingscote, Webb’s former partner and the father of the eldest of her three children, said: “The government has announced these regulations but they haven’t implemented them. They need to get on with it, get it done.”

During the inquest the jury heard Parke had been banned from carrying out BBLs in two areas of England because of his unsafe practices, but had been able to work elsewhere. Kingscote said: “We want to see prohibition orders recognised nationally rather than locally.”

Ashton Collins, the director of Save Face, a register of aesthetic practitioners, said it had taken too long for the proposed law changes to be drafted. She expressed concern there would be a rise in the number of people trying to get BBLs and other procedures before any changes came into effect.
after newsletter promotion
“We are seeing a huge rise in adverts from unscrupulous and unsafe providers offering Black Friday and Christmas special offers,” Collins said.

During the inquest, jurors were told the filler may have got into Webb’s system when a blood vessel was damaged during the BBL. In her final messages to family as she underwent the treatment, Webb said she was in pain, writing: “OMG – it kills.”

Police said they had found many other people who had suffered after treatment by Parke and were confident they would have brought a case of gross negligence manslaughter against him, but he died earlier this year.
The jury said in its findings that Webb died from “complications arising from BBL procedure”.
The senior coroner Katy Skerrett said she would be writing a “preventing future deaths report” detailing her concerns about the lack of regulation in the aesthetics industry.

A spokesperson for the Department of Health and Social Care said: “The government is already taking strict action to protect people from rogue operators. We have set out tough new proposals to restrict liquid Brazilian butt lifts and other body filler procedures to doctors, while ensuring other high-risk cosmetic procedures can only be carried out by appropriately qualified healthcare professionals.

“Those who break the rules risk criminal enforcement and unlimited fines. We are pressing ahead with these reforms, with draft regulations already out for consultation and the required period of parliamentary scrutiny scheduled for spring 2027.”
